summary: Defines TLS 1.3 cipher suites that provide authentication and integrity using HMAC but do not encrypt the data. They are not for general use, but can suit Internet of Things and constrained settings where confidentiality is not needed and cost matters. The document includes examples of such use cases. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: TLS 1.3 normally both encrypts and authenticates a connection. This RFC defines two TLS 1.3 cipher suites that authenticate the peer and detect tampering but leave the data readable by anyone on the path. They are meant for closed or industrial systems where the data is not secret and the device is too small or too slow to encrypt, and they come with the warning that no confidentiality is provided at all.

questions: when do you not need tls encryption
what is a tls integrity-only cipher suite
subtitle: Two TLS 1.3 cipher suites that authenticate and protect integrity without encrypting anything.

tldr.problem: Some industrial and Internet of Things devices must check that a message is genuine and unaltered, but carry data that is not secret, and they have too little processing power or memory to encrypt it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9150 defines two TLS 1.3 cipher suites, TLS_SHA256_SHA256 and TLS_SHA384_SHA384, that use an HMAC to protect the integrity of every record and to authenticate the peer, while leaving the record payload unencrypted.
tldr.outcome: The two cipher suites are registered with IANA so that implementations can interoperate, but the document is an independent submission that the IETF has not endorsed, both suites are marked as not recommended in the registry, and the RFC requires a threat model and a threat analysis before they are used.

today: RFC 9150 is an Informational document published in April 2022 as an independent submission. The IETF has not endorsed it and it carries no IETF consensus, and it has not been obsoleted. IANA has registered both cipher suites in the TLS Cipher Suites registry with the DTLS-OK flag set and the Recommended flag clear, and the RFC requires that they never be enabled by default.

sections.title: Why a Cipher Suite Without Encryption
sections.content:
There are several use cases in which communications privacy is not strictly needed, although the authenticity of the transport still is. In industrial automation, for example, there could be TCP or UDP communications that command a robotic arm to move a certain distance at a certain speed. Without authenticity guarantees an attacker could modify the packets to change the movement of the arm, potentially causing physical damage, yet the motion control commands are not always sensitive information, so there is no requirement to provide confidentiality. An Internet of Things (IoT) example with no strong confidentiality requirement is the reporting of weather information, where message authenticity is still required to keep the message intact.

There is no requirement to encrypt messages in environments where the information is not confidential, such as when there is no intellectual property associated with the process, or where the threat model does not indicate outsider attacks, as in a closed system. This does not apply equally to every case: a robotic arm might be used in one process with no intellectual property and in another process that does contain it. A user or system developer therefore has to examine both the sensitivity of the data and the threat model to decide whether encryption is needed before deploying equipment and protections.

Many of these systems also have a strong requirement for low latency, and several classes of IoT device have limited processing capability. They still gain a lot from using TLS 1.3 for secure communications. Given the reduced need for confidentiality, this document describes TLS 1.3 cipher suites that keep data integrity without confidentiality.

Two limits are stated up front. These cipher suites are not meant for general use, because they do not meet the confidentiality and privacy goals of TLS, and they should only be used where confidentiality and privacy are not a concern and where there are constraints on using cipher suites that provide the full set of security properties. The approach is not endorsed by the IETF and has no IETF consensus; it is presented to enable interoperable implementation of a reduced-security mechanism that provides authentication and message integrity without supporting confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: Some machines only need to know that a message really came from the right sender and was not altered on the way. If the message itself is not secret, encryption adds cost without adding much. This RFC describes a way to run TLS in that reduced mode, and it says plainly that the result is weaker and not endorsed by the IETF.

sections.title: Where These Cipher Suites Apply
sections.content:
The two cipher suites, based on Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) SHAs, are intended for a small limited set of applications where confidentiality requirements are relaxed and minimizing the number of cryptographic algorithms is a priority. The document gives five example use cases.

  • Industrial automation. Data sent to unmanned machines that execute repetitive tasks often does not convey private information. A robotic arm painting the body of a car is one piece of equipment in a multi-step process; the arm's movements are unlikely to be a trade secret even where other parts of the manufacturing might be sensitive, and the mixing of the paint is done by different equipment. Nearly every communication interaction still has strong data authenticity requirements.
  • Fine-grained time updates. Motion systems rely on time synchronization to execute properly. Time updates are essentially public, so there is no privacy threat, but authenticity still matters: maliciously modified time data can cause anything from denial of service to physical damage. The updates are fine-grained, so latency has to be very low.
  • Alarm data. Industrial control sensors send alarm information when a condition is met, such as a temperature crossing a threshold. The reading gives an attacker little to exploit, but being able to modify it would let an attacker raise false alarms or cover up the traces of an attack. These sensors are often low-powered devices that might struggle to process encrypted and authenticated data, and some are cost sensitive enough that encryption is out of reach.
  • Railway commands. In railway control systems no confidentiality requirement applies to the command exchange between an interlocking controller and a railway equipment controller, such as a point controller on a tram track whose position is publicly available. Integrity and authenticity are vital, since changing the target position of a point could derail a passing train. Flight-data recording of safety-related traffic also requires authenticity-only ciphers, because the recording is analyzed by a third party after an accident, and that party has to extract the safety-related commands from it.
  • Civil aviation. Pilots send and receive messages to and from ground control, such as route-of-flight updates, weather information, controller and pilot communication and airline back-office traffic. Air Traffic Control receives surveillance data that depends on downlink reports from the aircraft's avionics. The data gives an attacker little to exploit, but modifying it could put an aircraft on the wrong flight trajectory or delay flights, damage property or harm life.

The document also notes that memory, performance and processing implications of any algorithm are highly dependent on hardware and software architecture, so although these cipher suites may provide performance benefits they will not necessarily do so in all cases. In some use cases third-party inspection of the data is specifically needed, which the lack of confidentiality also supports.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are all cases where the content is not secret but the sender still has to be certain. Motion commands to a robot arm, time updates for a motion system, sensor alarms, railway point commands, and messages between aircraft and ground control. In several of them the device is small, slow or cheap enough that encrypting every message is a real burden.

sections.title: The Two Cipher Suites
sections.content:
The cryptographic negotiation specified in RFC 8446, Section 4.1.1, stays the same, with the addition of two cipher suites: TLS_SHA256_SHA256 {0xC0,0xB4} and TLS_SHA384_SHA384 {0xC0,0xB5}.

In TLS 1.3 a cipher suite name denotes the Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithm used for record protection and the hash algorithm used with the HMAC-based Key Derivation Function (HKDF). The cipher suites here are defined in a similar way, but they use the HMAC authentication tag to model the AEAD interface, because only an HMAC is provided for record protection, without encryption. They allow SHA-256 or SHA-384 to be used as the HMAC for data integrity protection as well as for the HKDF. The authentication mechanisms are unchanged; the intent is only to update the cipher suites so that the need for confidentiality is relaxed.

One restriction follows directly. Since these cipher suites do not support confidentiality, they MUST NOT be used with authentication and key exchange methods that rely on confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal TLS 1.3 cipher suite names an encryption method and a hash. These two name a hash only, and the code that expects an encryption method is given a message authentication code in its place. The rest of the handshake is untouched, but the suites cannot be combined with any key exchange that depends on keeping the handshake secret.

sections.title: How a Record Is Protected
sections.content:
Record payload protection as defined in RFC 8446 is retained in modified form. Because hash algorithms are used instead of AEAD algorithms, confidentiality protection of the record payload is not provided. Since there is no encryption to be done at the record layer, the operations Protect and Unprotect take the place of AEAD-Encrypt and AEAD-Decrypt.

Because integrity protection covers the full record, the encrypted_record in the TLSCiphertext and the additional_data input to protected_data stay as they are in RFC 8446. The length of the TLSCiphertext is the length of the encoded TLSInnerPlaintext plus 32 for TLS_SHA256_SHA256, or plus 48 for TLS_SHA384_SHA384. The protected record is the concatenation of the TLSInnerPlaintext with the resulting HMAC, so the encrypted_record field is set to TLSInnerPlaintext || HMAC(write_key, nonce || additional_data || TLSInnerPlaintext), where the nonce is the per-record nonce from RFC 8446. The DTLS 1.3 form uses the DTLSInnerPlaintext and the per-record nonce from DTLS 1.3. The record validation order of RFC 8446 is unchanged. The Protect and Unprotect operations provide the integrity protection using HMAC SHA-256 or HMAC SHA-384. Because the plaintext is not encrypted, record padding does not hide the plaintext size, although it can still be included.

The error alerts of RFC 8446 also stay the same, with two points worth noting. The bad_record_mac alert can now occur for a record whose message authentication code cannot be validated, and since there is no record encryption, it occurs only when the HMAC fails to verify. The decrypt_error alert occurs when the signature or message authentication code cannot be validated during the handshake, not for an error in validating record HMACs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record is sent as the data followed by a tag computed from the data, the connection keys and a per-record number. The tag is checked on arrival, and a mismatch is an error. Because nothing is encrypted, the padding that hides the length of a message in ordinary TLS no longer hides anything, and a reader can also see how long each message is.

sections.title: The Key Schedule
sections.content:
The key derivation process for the integrity-only cipher suites remains the same as in RFC 8446. The only difference is that the keys used to protect the tunnel apply to the negotiated HMAC SHA-256 or HMAC SHA-384 ciphers. The traffic key material, that is client_write_key, client_write_iv, server_write_key and server_write_iv, MUST be calculated as per RFC 8446, Section 7.3.

The key lengths and Initialization Vectors for these cipher suites follow the hash output lengths. For TLS_SHA256_SHA256 both the key length and the IV length are 32 bytes; for TLS_SHA384_SHA384 both are 48 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The keys and the per-record nonce are derived exactly as in TLS 1.3, so only the algorithm applied at the end of the derivation changes. The size of the key and of the nonce follows the size of the hash: 32 bytes with SHA-256 and 48 bytes with SHA-384.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Except for confidentiality and privacy, the security considerations of RFC 8446 and RFC 5246 apply. Because the cipher suites provide no confidentiality, they must only be used where there are no confidentiality or privacy requirements, and the runtime memory must be able to support authenticity-only cryptographic constructs.

The loss of privacy is spelled out. The record layer is not encrypted when these cipher suites are used, and neither is the handshake. The information carried in the handshake, which includes both the server and client certificates, is integrity protected but sent unencrypted, and other TLS extensions in the server's EncryptedExtensions message are only integrity protected. Any private Pre-Shared Key (PSK) data MUST NOT be sent in the handshake while using these cipher suites. Since PSKs may be loaded externally, the cipher suites can be used with the 0-RTT handshake of RFC 8446, with the same security implications discussed there.

Application protocols built on TLS or DTLS, such as HTTP, may have implicit assumptions of data confidentiality, and any such assumption is invalidated by these cipher suites. That applies to anything sent over the application-data channel, for example bearer tokens in HTTP, so data requiring confidentiality MUST NOT be sent with them.

Two further points concern the algorithm. The limits on key usage for AEAD-based ciphers in RFC 8446 do not apply, because these cipher suites are not AEAD, but the general security properties of HMACs discussed in RFC 2104 and in the keyed-hash analysis of Bellare, Canetti and Krawczyk apply, as do the considerations on algorithm strength based on HMAC key length and truncation length described in RFC 4868. Until further cryptanalysis demonstrates limits on HMAC key usage, general practice recommends that implementations limit the lifetime of the HMAC keys and invoke a key update as described in RFC 8446 before reaching that limit.

DTLS 1.3 has a mechanism for encrypting the record sequence numbers. Since these cipher suites do not use encryption, the record sequence numbers are sent unencrypted, and the procedure for DTLS record sequence number protection applies no protection for these cipher suites. Finally, given the lack of confidentiality, these cipher suites MUST NOT be enabled by default. Since they are meant to serve the IoT market, any IoT endpoint that uses them has to be explicitly configured with a policy of non-confidential communications.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing on the wire is secret with these cipher suites, not even the certificates in the handshake, so anything that must stay private cannot be sent this way. The suites must be turned on deliberately and never by default. What they do give is a check that the peer is who it claims to be and that nobody altered the messages in flight.

viz.caption: THE FIVE USE CASES GIVEN IN THE RFC

items.title: Industrial automation
items.text: Motion commands to equipment such as a robotic arm: the content is not secret, but a changed command could cause physical damage.

items.title: Fine-grained time updates
items.text: Time synchronization for motion systems: the updates are public, but modified time data can cause harm.

items.title: Alarm data
items.text: Sensor readings that trigger alarms: little to exploit, but altering them raises false alarms or hides an attack.

items.title: Railway commands
items.text: Commands to point controllers: publicly visible positions, but changing them could derail a train.

items.title: Civil aviation
items.text: Messages between aircraft and ground control: modifying them could put an aircraft on the wrong trajectory.

items.label: TLS_SHA256_SHA256
items.desc: HMAC SHA-256 for record integrity and for the key derivation function. Registered as DTLS-OK, not recommended.

items.desc: HMAC SHA-384 for record integrity and for the key derivation function. Registered as DTLS-OK, not recommended.
